content.title: HTTP Requests and Responses
content.objective: Explain GET and POST methods and distinguish between 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx response status categories.
content.overview: HTTP powers nearly every interaction on the web, from loading a page to submitting a form. In this lesson you'll learn how the client-server request/response cycle works, how the two most common HTTP methods—GET and POST—differ in purpose and behavior, and how to read HTTP status codes to quickly diagnose whether a request succeeded, failed because of something the client did, or failed because the server broke. By the end, you'll be able to look at a request or a status code and immediately say what it means.
learning_objectives: Describe the HTTP client-server request/response cycle and identify the parts of a request and response
Explain the purpose, safety, and idempotency of the GET method, including how it sends data via the URL query string
Explain the purpose, body usage, and idempotency of the POST method, including how it submits data to the server
Distinguish between 2xx (success), 4xx (client error), and 5xx (server error) status code categories
Identify what common status codes (200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500, 502, 503) mean in practice
content.audience: Beginner web developers who are comfortable using a browser and basic HTML, and want to understand how the web communicates under the hood

sections.title: Why HTTP Requests and Responses Matter
sections.content:
### The web runs on a conversation
Every time you load a page, submit a form, or an app fetches data, your browser (the **client**) and a web server are having a structured conversation called **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). HTTP is an application-layer, client-server protocol: the client opens a connection and sends a **request**, then waits for the server to send back a **response** [S4]. HTTP is also **stateless** — by default the server doesn't remember anything between two separate requests [S4].

Clients and servers exchange individual messages rather than a continuous stream: messages sent by the client are *requests*, and messages sent back are *responses* [S5].

### Analogy: ordering at a counter
Think of HTTP like ordering at a counter. You (the client) walk up and either:
- **Ask to see something** ("Can I see the menu?") — this is like **GET**, you're just retrieving information.
- **Hand over a form or an order** ("Here's my order slip with my choices written on it") — this is like **POST**, you're submitting data for the server to process.

The cashier's reply — "Here you go," "Sorry, we don't have that," or "Our kitchen is down" — maps directly to HTTP **status codes**: success, client error, or server error.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to read both halves of that conversation fluently.

sections.title: What You Need Before Starting
sections.content:
### Assumed knowledge
- Basic familiarity with URLs (e.g., `https://example.com/contact`)
- Basic HTML, especially the idea of a `<form>` element
- Comfort opening browser developer tools (optional but helpful for the activity)

### Key vocabulary you'll use
| Term | Quick definition |
|---|---|
| Client | The program initiating the request (usually a browser) [S5] |
| Server | The program that listens for requests and sends responses [S10] |
| Request method ("HTTP verb") | A word describing what the client wants to do, e.g., `GET`, `POST` [S3] |
| Status code | A 3-digit number telling the client whether the request succeeded or failed [S3] |
| Header | Metadata about the request or response, sent as key:value pairs [S3][S4] |
| Body | Optional data attached to a message, such as form data in a request or HTML in a response [S3] |

No prior HTTP knowledge is required — we build everything up from these basics.

sections.title: GET and POST: Purpose, Safety, and Idempotency
sections.content:
### Anatomy of a request and response
An HTTP request has a start-line (method + target + protocol version), headers, and an optional body; a response has a status line (protocol + status code + reason phrase), headers, and an optional body [S3][S5]. HTTP defines a set of **request methods** to indicate the purpose of a request and what's expected if it succeeds; the two most common are **GET** and **POST** [S4][S8].

### GET: retrieve data
The `GET` method requests a representation of a specified resource. Requests using GET **should only retrieve data and should not contain a request body** — the semantics of sending a body with GET are undefined, and some servers will reject it with a 4xx error [S6][S7][S8]. Instead, GET sends parameters through the **URL query string** (the part after `?`), often as `key=value` pairs [S6][S7]:

```http
GET /contact?name=alex HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
```

**GET's three defining properties** [S6][S7][S8]:
- **Safe** — Yes. It does not alter server state.
- **Idempotent** — Yes. Making the same GET request once or ten times produces the same result and has the same effect.
- **Cacheable** — Yes. Browsers and intermediaries can store and reuse GET responses.

### POST: submit data
The `POST` method submits an entity (data) to the specified resource, often causing a change in state or side effects on the server, such as creating a new record [S8]. Formally, POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed data according to that resource's own semantics [S10] - creating a resource is one common use, but POST is equally used to submit forms, post messages, or trigger actions such as checkout. Unlike GET, POST data is sent in the **request body**, not the URL [S9]:

```http
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 13

say=Hi&to=Mom
```

**POST's defining properties** [S8]:
- **Safe** — No. It is expected to change server state.
- **Idempotent** — No, by default. Submitting the same POST twice (e.g., resubmitting an order form) can create two resources instead of one.
- **Cacheable** — Only conditionally, when the response explicitly provides freshness information and a matching `Content-Location` header [S8]; in practice, POST responses are generally not cached.

### GET vs. POST at a glance
| Property | GET | POST |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Retrieve a representation of a resource [S6] | Submit data to be processed, often creating/changing a resource [S8] |
| Where data goes | URL query string [S6][S7] | Request body [S9] |
| Has a request body? | No (undefined/discouraged) [S6] | Yes [S3][S9] |
| Safe (no server state change) | Yes [S6][S7][S8] | No [S8] |
| Idempotent (repeat = same effect) | Yes [S6][S7][S8] | No [S8] |
| Cacheable | Yes [S6][S7][S8] | Conditional only [S8] |
| Visible in browser history/URL | Yes [S6] | No [S9] |

The method purposes, safety, and idempotency described above are formally defined in **RFC 9110**, the current IETF standard for HTTP semantics (successor to the original RFC 2616); detailed caching behavior is further specified in the companion standard RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching). MDN's documentation draws on both [S1][S2][S10].

### Connecting to HTML you already know
If you've written a `<form>` in HTML, you've likely set (or seen) its `method` attribute:
```html
<form method="get" action="/search">...</form>
<form method="post" action="/users">...</form>
```
`method="get"` makes the browser submit the form's fields as a URL query string (exactly the GET behavior above); `method="post"` makes the browser submit them in the request body (exactly the POST behavior above). This is the same GET/POST distinction you just learned — just expressed as an HTML attribute instead of a raw HTTP message.

sections.title: Status Code Categories: 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx
sections.content:
### The structure: first digit = category
HTTP response status codes are 3-digit numbers that indicate whether a specific HTTP request was successfully completed [S1][S2]. The **first digit** tells you the category; responses are grouped into **five classes** [S1][S2][S4]:

| Range | Class | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1xx (100–199) | Informational | Request received, continuing process (rarely seen directly) [S1] |
| 2xx (200–299) | **Successful** | The request was received, understood, and accepted [S1] |
| 3xx (300–399) | Redirection | Further action (usually a follow-up request) is needed [S1] |
| 4xx (400–499) | **Client error** | The request sent by the client was invalid [S1] |
| 5xx (500–599) | **Server error** | The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request [S1] |

These categories and the codes within them are defined by **RFC 9110** [S1][S2]. If you ever see a code not in the standard list, it's a non-standard, server-specific response [S1].

### 2xx — Success
- **200 OK** — The request succeeded; meaning depends on the method. For GET, the resource is fetched and returned in the body; for POST, a resource describing the result of the action is returned [S1][S2].
- **201 Created** — A new resource was successfully created, commonly returned after a successful POST [S1][S3]. Example: creating a user returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource [S3].
- **204 No Content** — The request succeeded, but there is no additional content to send in the response body (common after a successful delete or an autosave) [S1][S10].

### 4xx — Client error (something wrong with the request)
- **400 Bad Request** — The server cannot or will not process the request due to a client-side problem, e.g., malformed syntax [S1][S2].
- **401 Unauthorized** — Semantically means "unauthenticated": the client must authenticate itself before getting the requested response [S1][S2].
- **403 Forbidden** — The client's identity is known, but it doesn't have access rights to the content [S1][S2].
- **404 Not Found** — The server cannot find the requested resource [S1][S2].

### 5xx — Server error (something wrong on the server)
- **500 Internal Server Error** — A generic error meaning the server hit a problem it doesn't have a more specific 5xx code for [S1][S2].
- **501 Not Implemented** — The request method isn't supported by the server (note: GET and HEAD must always be supported) [S1][S2].
- **502 Bad Gateway** — The server, acting as a gateway/proxy, got an invalid response from an upstream server [S1][S2].
- **503 Service Unavailable** — The server is not ready to handle the request, often due to overload or maintenance [S1][S2].

### The core distinction
- **2xx** = "It worked."
- **4xx** = "*You* (the client) sent something wrong." Fix the request.
- **5xx** = "*I* (the server) broke." The client usually can't fix this by changing the request.

sections.title: Worked Examples: Reading Real Requests and Responses
sections.content:
### Example 1 — A GET request and its 200 response
Request:
```http
GET /contact HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.6.0
Accept: */*
```
Response:
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 1234

<!doctype html>
<!-- page content -->
```
*Walkthrough:* The method is `GET`, so no body is sent; the resource path and query (if any) carry all the needed info [S6][S7]. The server responds `200 OK` because the resource was found and returned in the body [S1][S6].

### Example 2 — A POST request and its 201 response
Request (submitting a form that creates a user):
```http
POST /users HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 13

say=Hi&to=Mom
```
Response:
```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: http://example.com/users/123

{"message": "New user created", "user": {"id": 123}}
```
*Walkthrough:* The data (`say=Hi&to=Mom`) is in the **body**, not the URL [S9]. The server used `201 Created` (not just `200`) because a brand-new resource was made, and it tells the client exactly where via the `Location` header [S1][S3].

### Example 3 — Diagnosing an error
You POST a login form with the wrong password and get:
```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
```
*Walkthrough:* `4` as the first digit → client error. Specifically `401` means the client hasn't successfully authenticated [S1][S2] — you'd fix this by resubmitting with correct credentials, not by reporting a bug.

Now compare: your request is fine, but the server's database crashed:
```http
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
```
*Walkthrough:* `5` as the first digit → server error. The server isn't ready to handle any request right now [S1][S2] — retrying later (or reporting to the ops team) is the right move, not editing your request.

sections.title: Where This Shows Up in Real Development
sections.content:
- **Search bars and links** use `GET` because they only fetch data — this is why you can bookmark or refresh a search results page safely [S6][S8].
- **Login, checkout, and "create" forms** use `POST` because they submit data that changes server state (new order, new account) [S8][S9].
- **APIs** (built on the Fetch API or similar) rely on status codes so client code can branch logic: show data on `200`, show a validation message on `400`, prompt re-login on `401`, and show a generic "try again later" on `5xx` [S1][S5].
- Browser **dev tools** (Network tab) let you inspect the exact method, headers, body, and status code of every request your page makes — the fastest way to debug "why didn't my form work?"

sections.title: Practical Activity: Classify Real Requests and Status Codes
sections.content:
### Step 1 — Inspect a real GET request
1. Open any website in your browser.
2. Open DevTools (F12) → **Network** tab, then reload the page.
3. Click the first HTML request. Note the **Method** (should be `GET`) and the **Status** code (should be `200`).

### Step 2 — Trigger a POST and a 4xx
1. Open `https://httpbin.org/forms/post` — a public test form built for exactly this kind of practice.
2. Fill in any values and submit it with the Network tab open.
3. Click the request in the Network tab: confirm **Method = POST**, note the **Request Payload/body** (your submitted data), and check the status — it should return `200 OK` with your data echoed back as JSON.
4. (Optional) To see a real 401 safely, open `https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/testuser/testpass` in a new (ideally private/incognito) tab. When the browser's login prompt appears, enter any *wrong* username or password and check the Network tab — the response will be `401 Unauthorized`, which is exactly how a real login form's server-side check would respond to bad credentials. Avoid testing wrong passwords on live accounts you actually use, since repeated failed logins can trigger lockouts or security alerts.

### Step 3 — Classify
For each scenario below, write down GET or POST, and the status category (2xx/4xx/5xx):
- Fetching a product page by clicking a link → ______
- Submitting a "Create account" form successfully → ______
- Requesting a page that was deleted (`/old-page`) → ______
- Hitting an API during server maintenance → ______

**Expected outcome:** Page/link = GET, 2xx. Successful signup = POST, 2xx (likely 201). Deleted page = GET, 4xx (404). Maintenance = 5xx (503), independent of method.

**Self-check:** Can you explain *why* resubmitting the same GET request is always safe, but resubmitting the same POST form (e.g., double-clicking "Submit") could create a duplicate order? If yes, you've grasped idempotency [S6][S7][S8].

sections.title: Knowledge check
sections.content: Answer all 6 questions below to confirm you can explain GET and POST and distinguish 2xx/4xx/5xx status categories.

sections.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
sections.content:
### What you learned
- HTTP is a client-server, request/response protocol: clients send requests, servers send responses [S4][S5].
- **GET** retrieves data, sends parameters via the URL query string, has no body, and is **safe**, **idempotent**, and **cacheable** [S6][S7][S8].
- **POST** submits data in the **request body**, often changes server state, and is **not safe** and **not idempotent** by default [S8][S9].
- Status codes are 3-digit numbers whose first digit sets the category: **2xx = success**, **4xx = client error**, **5xx = server error** [S1][S2][S4].
- Common codes to remember: `200 OK`, `201 Created` (2xx); `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `403 Forbidden`, `404 Not Found` (4xx); `500 Internal Server Error`, `502 Bad Gateway`, `503 Service Unavailable` (5xx) [S1][S2].

### Next steps
Try inspecting more of your own app's requests in DevTools, and look up the 3xx (redirection) and PUT/PATCH/DELETE methods to round out your HTTP vocabulary [S8].

claims.note: RFC 9110 as the current standard is supported, but no retrieved evidence states that it is the 'successor to RFC 2616' or that RFC 9111 is a 'companion standard' for caching — those specifics are unsupported by the given sources.

claims.claim: HTTP response status codes are 3-digit numbers that indicate whether a specific HTTP request was successfully completed, and are grouped into five classes based on the first digit.
claims.evidence_quote: Responses are grouped in five classes: Informational responses (100–199) Successful responses (200–299) Redirection messages (300–399) Client error responses (400–499) Server error responses (500–599)

claims.claim: 2xx status codes mean the request was received, understood, and accepted (Successful).
claims.evidence_quote: Successful responses (200–299)
claims.note: Evidence confirms 2xx = Successful, but the specific phrasing 'received, understood, and accepted' is RFC wording not present verbatim in the retrieved passages.

claims.claim: 4xx status codes mean the request sent by the client was invalid (Client error).
claims.evidence_quote: The server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error

claims.claim: 5xx status codes mean the server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request (Server error).
claims.evidence_quote: The server has encountered a situation it does not know how to handle.

claims.claim: 201 Created indicates a new resource was successfully created, commonly returned after a successful POST, e.g. creating a user returns 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource.
claims.evidence_quote: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json Location: http://example.com/users/123

claims.claim: 204 No Content means the request succeeded but there is no additional content to send in the response body, common after a successful delete or an autosave.
claims.evidence_quote: All 1xx (Informational), 204 (No Content), and 304 (Not Modified) responses do not include content.
claims.note: Core definition supported; the added examples 'successful delete or an autosave' are not stated in the retrieved evidence.

claims.claim: 401 Unauthorized semantically means 'unauthenticated': the client must authenticate itself before getting the requested response.
claims.evidence_quote: Although the HTTP standard specifies 'unauthorized', semantically this response means 'unauthenticated'. That is, the client must authenticate itself to get the requested response.

claims.claim: 403 Forbidden means the client's identity is known, but it doesn't have access rights to the content.
claims.evidence_quote: The client does not have access rights to the content; that is, it is unauthorized, so the server is refusing to give the requested resource. Unlike 401 Unauthorized, the client's identity is known to the server.

claims.claim: 501 Not Implemented means the request method isn't supported by the server; GET and HEAD must always be supported.
claims.evidence_quote: The request method is not supported by the server and cannot be handled. The only methods that servers are required to support (and therefore must not return this code) are GET and HEAD.

qc_instructional.summary: This is a well-researched, logically sequenced lesson with strong real-world grounding (DevTools + httpbin.org activity, worked HTTP message examples) and an assessment that maps cleanly onto the stated objective. Its main weaknesses are pacing-related: the two core concept sections and the hands-on activity each carry more content/steps than their allotted minutes can realistically absorb for a true beginner, and pervasive inline citation brackets add unnecessary clutter to beginner-facing prose.
qc_instructional.methodology: Score = sum of ten rubric criteria scored 0-10 by an independent instructional-design review: Learning objective alignment, Explanation clarity, Logical sequence, Concept completeness, Quality of examples, Practical applicability, Student engagement, Knowledge-check relevance, Difficulty progression, 45-minute time compliance. The time-compliance criterion is forced to 0 by code when section minutes exceed 45. Deterministic checks add issues for missing required sections, fewer than 4 knowledge checks, or objective parts with no knowledge check. Verdict: 'Needs revision' if any critical issue, any objective part not covered, the 45-minute limit is exceeded, or score < 70; 'Passed' if score >= 85 and no high-severity issue; otherwise 'Passed with recommendations'.

rubric.note: The stated objective (GET/POST + 2xx/4xx/5xx) is fully and directly addressed in concepts-1, concepts-2, examples, activity, and knowledge check. However, the lesson's own 'Learning objectives' list adds two sub-objectives not in the original ask — describing the full request/response cycle and memorizing 9 specific status codes (200/201/400/401/403/404/500/502/503) — which expands scope beyond what was assigned and puts extra pressure on the 45-minute budget.

The counter-ordering analogy and the GET/POST comparison table are genuinely clear. Clarity is reduced by dense inline citation brackets (e.g., '[S4]', '[S7][S8]') scattered through almost every sentence of beginner-facing prose, which adds visual noise and is never explained to the learner (what is 'S4'?). Formal terms like 'safe' and 'idempotent' are used heavily before being distilled into a single plain-language takeaway sentence.

Intro → prerequisites → GET/POST → status codes → worked examples → real-world applications → activity → check → summary is a clean, standard progression with no backward references or out-of-order dependencies.

GET and POST are covered with purpose, data placement, safety, idempotency, and cacheability; status codes are covered by category and by specific common code. Gaps: no plain-language definition of 'idempotent' is given before the term is used repeatedly, and the security implication of GET placing data in a URL (visible in history/logs — don't use for passwords) is listed as a fact in the table but never explained as a reason to care.

Three well-chosen worked examples (GET/200, POST/201, 401 vs 503 contrast) directly mirror the lesson's core distinctions. One example has a content mismatch: Example 2 is narrated as 'submitting a form that creates a user' but the body shown is `say=Hi&to=Mom`, which reads as an unrelated greeting-card payload rather than user-creation fields, undercutting the example's realism.

The 'Where This Shows Up' section and the DevTools/httpbin.org activity ground the concepts in things beginners can touch immediately (search bars, login forms, Network tab debugging), which is exactly the kind of transfer a beginner audience needs.
Analogy, hands-on browser inspection, a public test form, and a self-check reflection question all actively involve the learner rather than just presenting facts.

All 6 questions map directly to the stated objective (GET properties, POST non-idempotency, data placement, 201, 400, 500) with plausible distractors. Minor gap: 403 Forbidden is taught but never tested or distinguished from 401 in any question, and no question explicitly forces comparison across all three categories in one item.

Moves from everyday analogy → formal definitions → comparison table → worked examples → open-ended classification activity → mixed-format assessment, a sensible easy-to-hard arc appropriate for beginners.

Several sections are under-budgeted for their actual content load: concepts-1 packs anatomy, GET properties, a code block, POST properties, a code block, a 7-row comparison table, an RFC aside, and an HTML form tie-in into 8 minutes; concepts-2 packs 5 classes + 11 individual codes into 8 minutes; and the activity asks a beginner to learn DevTools Network tab navigation, visit two-to-three external sites, submit a form, optionally test incognito basic-auth, and classify 4 scenarios in just 6 minutes. These are realistically 10-15 minute tasks for first-time learners, making the stated 44-minute total optimistic.

qc_instructional.clarity: Core explanations are generally clear and well-structured, aided by a strong opening analogy and a comprehensive GET-vs-POST comparison table. The main clarity drag is the pervasive inline citation bracketing (e.g., '[S6][S7][S8]') embedded directly in beginner-facing sentences, which adds visual clutter and is never explained to the reader, and the fact that formal vocabulary ('safe', 'idempotent') is used extensively before being reduced to a single plain-language sentence a true beginner could hold onto.
qc_instructional.example_quality: The three worked examples are well-chosen and map cleanly onto the lesson's core distinctions (GET/200, POST/201, 401-vs-503 contrast), with full HTTP messages and walkthroughs that connect every line back to a taught concept. The one weakness is Example 2, where the request body (`say=Hi&to=Mom`) doesn't semantically match its stated scenario ('a form that creates a user'), which could confuse a learner trying to map body fields to a real-world use case.
qc_instructional.activity_quality: The activity is strong in concept — real DevTools inspection plus a public test API (httpbin.org) gives authentic, low-risk hands-on practice, and the self-check question about idempotency is a good metacognitive close. Its weakness is scope-for-time: three distinct browser/site interactions (home site inspection, httpbin form POST, optional incognito 401 test) plus a 4-item classification exercise is too much to realistically complete in 6 minutes for someone opening DevTools for the first time.
qc_instructional.assessment_quality: The 6 knowledge-check questions align tightly with the objective and use a good mix of formats (MCQ, true/false, short free-response), with plausible, objective-relevant distractors (e.g., conflating GET with resource creation, confusing 4xx/5xx fault attribution). The main gaps are that 403 Forbidden is taught but never assessed, and the 4-minute time allotment is tight for two free-response questions plus reading six detailed explanations.

Why GET exposing data in the URL/browser history matters in practice (e.g., don't send passwords or sensitive data via GET) — the comparison table states this fact but doesn't explain its real-world consequence

A brief note distinguishing 401 (not authenticated) from 403 (authenticated but not authorized), since both are introduced but their difference is only implicit in the definitions and neither is tested

issues.original_text:
### Step 2 — Trigger a POST and a 4xx
1. Open `https://httpbin.org/forms/post` — a public test form built for exactly this kind of practice.
2. Fill in any values and submit it with the Network tab open.
3. Click the request in the Network tab: confirm **Method = POST**, note the **Request Payload/body** (your submitted data), and check the status — it should return `200 OK` with your data echoed back as JSON.
4. (Optional) To see a real 401 safely, open `https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/testuser/testpass` in a new (ideally private/incognito) tab. When the browser's login prompt appears, enter any *wrong* username or password and check the Network tab — the response will be `401 Unauthorized`, which is exactly how a real login form's server-side check would respond to bad credentials. Avoid testing wrong passwords on live accounts you actually use, since repeated failed logins can trigger lockouts or security alerts.
issues.suggested_text:
### Step 2 — Trigger a POST
1. Open `https://httpbin.org/forms/post` — a public test form built for exactly this kind of practice.
2. Fill in any values and submit it with the Network tab open.
3. Click the request in the Network tab: confirm **Method = POST**, note the **Request Payload/body** (your submitted data), and check the status — it should return `200 OK` with your data echoed back as JSON.

*Stretch step — do this only if you have extra time:* To see a real 401, open `https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/testuser/testpass` in a new private/incognito tab and enter a *wrong* username or password at the login prompt — the Network tab will show `401 Unauthorized`. Avoid testing wrong passwords on live accounts you actually use, since repeated failed logins can trigger lockouts.
